title: Predictive-resize snapping and progressive-density for virtualized table UX
creator: Ava Patel
description: Objective: design and validate a set of interaction patterns and visuals for column resizing, sorting/filtering affordances, and compact/expanded density modes in the virtualized table component. The focus is on preserving user intent across virtualization reflows (when offscreen rows/columns are re-materialized), providing a predictive resize snapping model to avoid surprise jumps, and introducing a progressive density scale that maintains legibility and tap targets while enabling 3 compactness tiers. Deliverables include high-fidelity prototypes, accessibility behavior spec, token recommendations, and a handoff-ready component spec for engineering.
background: Current virtualized table has two pain points: 1) when a user drags a column edge to resize, the virtualization reflow sometimes snaps the column to an unexpected width (due to measurement rounding and offscreen padding), breaking perceived control; 2) density options are binary (default/compact) and do not offer predictable intermediate steps for teams that need tighter layouts for dashboards. Multiple customer requests call for better control over column width persistence and a medium-density mode for high-cardinality data grids.
acceptance_criteria: Resize interaction: dragging a column edge shows a low-latency live preview with an alignment guideline and snaps to a predictable grid when crossing defined thresholds (4px, 8px, 16px).
Persistence: resized widths persist across pagination/virtualization cycles for the current session and are reconcilable with autosize operations.

Progressive density: provide three named density presets (Comfortable, Compact, Micro) with token values for row-height, vertical padding, and icon/text sizes and demonstrable readability at 14px body text.

Filtering/sorting UX: per-column filter chips show active filter counts, support multi-select chip interactions, and offer an inline sort caret that is reachable via keyboard without opening filter menus.

Accessibility: all interactions are operable with keyboard-only, provide screen-reader-friendly announcements for resize start/commit and density changes, and maintain 44px minimum touch targets unless in Micro mode (flagged and documented).
Engineering handoff: a single-page spec (tokens, CSS variables, interaction states) and a Figma prototype with comment-thread signoff from PM and Eng lead.
tasks: Audit current table component behaviors and collect failure repro steps with virtualization enabled
Sketch and iterate on predictive snapping heuristics and alignment guideline visuals
Prototype a live-resize HTML/CSS/JS demo to validate low-latency preview and persistence model
Design three density presets and map to existing design tokens (create delta tokens if needed)
Update filter chip visual language to include count badges and keyboard focus states
Write A11y spec: keyboard bindings, ARIA announcements, reduced-motion considerations
Handoff spec and run 30-minute sync with eng, PM, and accessibility reviewer
Address feedback and lock tokens for release branch
decisions: Use a predictive snapping grid with thresholds at increments of 4/8/16px to balance precision and discoverability
Persist resize state in-memory per session keyed by table id; long-term persistence deferred to separate storage ticket
Introduce a middle density (Compact) that reduces vertical padding by 30% and a Micro mode reserved for monitor-dense UIs with clear opt-in documentation
Filter chips will move from passive labels to actionable controls with inline keyboard focus and a count badge for multi-value filters
notes: We observed resize jitter is often caused by re-measure after virtualization buffer fills; engineering will expose a 'freeze-layout-during-drag' flag to block reflow while user is actively resizing.
Consider exposing 'density' as a top-level table prop so product teams can toggle presets without rewiring token maps.
Design tokens for Micro density must include an explicit warning in docs about touch target reductions and recommended usage scenarios.
